newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW-Asia stocks shudder at higher US rates.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW-Asia stocks shudder at higher US rates.

text.p: Asian stocks are in shock at the prospect of higher U.S. interest rates for the first time in more than two years, fund managers said.

"The reality that suddenly, for the first time in nearly three years, interest rates are going up, has frightened people," said Richard Nicholas, managing director at Hambro Pacific Fund Management Ltd in Hong Kong.
Asian-dedicated funds are flowing out of Hong Kong and southeast Asian stocks into markets in India and Taiwan, both of which are less rate sensitive than the rest of the region.

Testimony by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Thursday prompted widespread weakness in Asia, where many countries are tied to American monetary policy through currency links to the U.S. dollar.

Greenspan told Congress that the U.S. economy retains a "great deal of vigour," and warned that an immediate shift in monetary policy would not affect inflationary pressures until "late this year and in 1998."

Asian markets promptly slid across the board in anticipation of a 25-basis point rise in the federal funds rate to 5.50 percent at the March 25 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's policy-making arm.

"The markets are very jittery," said David Semple, regional strategist at Peregrine Asset Management in Hong Kong. "Anything more than 25 will take the market by surprise. Anything less than 25 will take the market by surprise," he said.
However, most Asian market players were expecting further rate increases following next week's possible move.

"If the Fed raises rates, it won't be a one-off. It'll be a series to 75 or 100 basis points depending on whether growth slows in response to the rate hikes or if inflation picks up," said Ophelia Tong, chief investment officer at National Mutual Funds Management in Hong Kong.
Hedge funds were reported to be active in Hong Kong, where index futures were rising to discount a combined rate increase of 75 basis points by December, Semple said.

"I don't know whether that's fully incorporated into the cash markets yet," Semple said. "My view is it's not. There is still potential downside purely on the U.S. interest rate story before you start to go into the bigger picture."
The bigger picture has darkened perceptibly, too.
Cheaper yen reduced borrowing costs for countries funding wide current accounts throughout Asia in 1996, a year marked by a slump in exports and declining economic growth.
Improvements in Asian current accounts deficits expected this year on the back of better exports will now be eroded by an increase in the cost of borrowing, Semple said.
"That momentum of yen-weakening seems to be running out of steam. People in yen short-term know the game will be up soon and they've been piling into U.S. dollar assets," he said.

Fund managers are moving money into India and Taiwan to escape the worst of the damage in Asia, where Hong Kong's stock market could slide further following recent consolidation, and where most other markets are drifting weaker.
Taiwan's red-hot stock market restricts foreign access and is driven largely by local retail investors, but, "India post-budget is worth a look," said Hambro Pacific's Nicholas.
"We've moved out of Hong Kong and into India," another fund manager said.
